shapes.text: So, with keys, one row can point at another. And it turns out those links only come in a few shapes.

names.text: One to many. Many to many. One to one. And the odd one out... a table that points at itself.

many.text: A customer can place lots of orders, but each order belongs to just one customer.

ends.text: Two bars by customers mean exactly one. A crow's foot and a circle by orders mean zero or many.

where-in.text: So which table holds the link?

list.text: Not customers. Ada's orders, one and twenty-five, would have to share one cell.

cell.text: Nothing can check a list like that, and every new order means editing Ada's row.

fk.text: So the foreign key goes on the many side. Each order stores one customer ID, and Ada's shows up twice.

repeat.text: That repetition isn't duplication. It IS the relationship.

cross-in.text: But what if both sides can have many?

cross.text: A student takes lots of courses, and a course has lots of students. Ada takes Math and History. Grace takes Math and Art.

tangle.text: The links cross, because neither side is the parent.

slot.text: Give students a course ID, and Ada's row has room for one. Math fits... so where does History go?

flip.text: Flip it, and Math has room for one student. Where does Grace go?

one-side.text: One foreign key always forces one side to be one.

pairing.text: So give every pairing its own row, in a third table: enrollments.

rows.text: Ada in Math is a row, Ada in History another, each with two foreign keys.

two.text: So the tangle becomes two plain one-to-manys.

named.text: That's a junction table. It's not a hack... it gives the relationship a name.

pair.text: And the pair of keys is the row's identity: student and course, together, make the primary key.

once.text: Enroll Linus in Math, and that's row forty-nine. Try it again? Postgres says no: that key already exists.

grade.text: The row can hold facts of its own, too, like a grade. Not on students, though: Ada got a B in Math and a C in History.

course.text: Not on courses either: Math gave Ada a B, and Grace a C.

belongs.text: It belongs to Ada in Math, on the pairing's own row.

one-in.text: The next shape splits one thing in two.

wide.text: Say a users table starts collecting profile details, like a display name and a bio.

empty.text: Lots of users, like Linus, never fill them in.

split.text: So the profile moves to its own table. Each user has zero or one profile, and each profile belongs to exactly one user.

side.text: The foreign key goes on the profile, the side that can't exist alone.

unique.text: But a foreign key alone won't keep it to one. It'll happily take a second profile for Ada.

unique-fix.text: Make that user ID unique, and the second one bounces. That's what makes it one to one.

self-in.text: The last shape needs only one table.

self.text: An employee has a manager, and the manager's an employee too. So the foreign key points back into its own table.

tree.text: Ada's the CEO, with no manager. Grace reports to Ada, and Mina reports to Grace.

deep.text: Each row stores only its own manager, and the chain runs as deep as it needs: five levels here, down to an intern.

alias.text: To read it, join the table to itself, as employee and as manager. A left join keeps Ada, with no manager.

guard.text: But a foreign key only checks that the manager exists. So what if Ada manages... Ada?

accepted.text: Postgres takes it. One row updated.

next.text: Keys guard the links between tables. To guard what goes in them, you need constraints.
